[MUQATIL:41:39-40/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | God’s created works make His oneness known, even though people do not see Him.
[MUQATIL:41:39-40/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The earth is dry, dusty, broken up, and without vegetation.
[MUQATIL:41:39-40/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Rain makes the dead earth live and sprout; it shakes with greenery and increases its plants.
[MUQATIL:41:39-40/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The One who revived earth after death will revive the dead in the Hereafter, teaching anyone who doubts resurrection.
[MUQATIL:41:39-40/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | God has power over resurrection and everything else.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p188#2/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatada describes the earth as gray and crumbling.
[TAB-FULL:v20p438/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The revival of barren land is evidence that God can raise the dead and restore them after they have decayed.
[TAB-FULL:v20p438/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada glosses the humbled earth as gray and broken.
[TAB-FULL:v20p438/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi glosses the humbled earth as dry and crumbling.
[TAB-FULL:v20p438/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | When rain from the sky falls on the barren land, it stirs as vegetation grows; the same wording appears in 22:5. | mentions 22:5
[TAB-FULL:v20p438/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid explains that the earth stirs with vegetation.
[TAB-FULL:v20p438/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The earth “swells” after rain. | mentions 22:5
[TAB-FULL:v20p438/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi also glosses “swelled” as “expanded.”
[TAB-FULL:v20p438/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says rain is recognized in the land's surface and swelling. | mentions 22:5
[TAB-FULL:v20p438/r9] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid associates the swelling with plants and says the earth rises before they sprout.
[TAB-FULL:v20p439/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The God who revives barren land and brings out plants by rain can revive dead human beings after their death.
[TAB-FULL:v20p439/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says that just as rain revives earth, water revives the dead between the two trumpet blasts on Resurrection Day.
[TAB-FULL:v20p439/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | God can revive creation after death and do anything He wills; nothing He intends defeats or eludes His power.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p387/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The earth is crumbling and changed, like hāmida.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p387/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The verb is also read with hamza as rabaʾat.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p387/r8] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Rabat means grew or swelled, while rabaʾat means rose as the ground lifts when plants are about to emerge.
[NAHHAS:v4p62/r10] NAHHAS, d. 338 · المازني | reports | Al-Māzinī supplies an implicit verb to govern what cannot begin independently, estimating كيف استقر زيد.
[NAHHAS:v4p62/r11] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | خاشعة is parsed as a circumstantial accusative.
[NAHHAS:v4p62/r12] NAHHAS, d. 338 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh derives ربت from ربا يربو and gives its dual as ربوان.
[NAHHAS:v4p62/r13] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans give the dual as ربيان and write ربا with yāʾ.
[NAHHAS:v4p62/r14] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | prefers | Abū Jaʿfar favors the Basran analysis, saying the Qurʾanic form supports it; Abū Isḥāq rebukes the Kufans for extending a spelling error to the dual. | mentions 30:39
[NAHHAS:v4p62/r15] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو جعفر | reports | A recitation attributed to Abū Jaʿfar has اهتزت وربأت, derived from the word for a lookout who rises to a high place.
[NAHHAS:v4p62/r16] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | ربأت means “rose,” from the verb for ascending to a high lookout position.
[NAHHAS:v4p62/r17] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | In لمحيي, the yāʾ loses its ḍamma because it is heavy, then a yāʾ is deleted where two sukūns meet.
[NAHHAS:v4p62/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh parses أن as a nominative subject; the preceding material licenses it despite his general rule against starting with أن.
[SULAMI:v2p220#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · عمرو بن عثمان المكي | reports | Amr ibn Uthman likens hearts to earth: God's mercy, gaze, and beneficence awaken hidden deposits, producing humility before God, awe among people, compassion, counsel, and lasting fear of sin; the One who revives these souls can revive inattentive hearts and those dead to service.
[THALABI:v8p297/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | A barren, dry earth revived by rain proves that the One who revives it can also revive the dead.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p183/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbi says the earth stirs with vegetation and rises through abundant yield.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p183/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The revived earth is observable evidence for deniers that God can raise the dead, reasoning from what is seen to what is unseen.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p183/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · قتادة | reports | Qatada glosses the earth as dusty and worn out.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p183/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi glosses the earth as dead and dry.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p183/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The earth is humbled by drought when abandoned, but flourishing and esteemed when inhabited.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p183/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the earth moves as plants emerge and rises beforehand; his reading reverses the stated order to “rose, then moved.”
[QUSHAYRI:v3p152/r10] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The One who revives dead earth can raise the dead, and He can also revive hearts with the light of care after spiritual slackness and veiling.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p152/r7] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | As rain revives parched winter earth, awareness of sin humbles hearts; God turns toward them, bringing the blessings of regret and forgiving their failures in sincerity.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p152/r8] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | When a servant lapses in spiritual practice or leaves the ground of obedience, God’s reminder brings lights of concord, restores the accustomed station, and makes the branch of fidelity fresh again.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p152/r9] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | If gnostics pause or suffer a veil because of bad etiquette, God’s caring regard makes their gardens of intimacy stir, their scenes of nearness green, and their impediments retreat.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:41:39-43/r1] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The earth is barren and dusty, with no plants.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:41:39-43/r2] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The earth moves with vegetation, swells and rises, then splits open to produce plants.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p108/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | A simile gains finesse when it finds a likeness across different kinds of things, carrying an image from a distant domain into a new one.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p108/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Even the familiar eye-and-narcissus comparison spans different kinds; comparisons of the Pleiades to a flowering grape cluster, silver bridle, or necklace are more particular examples.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p108/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The more distant the compared things, the more astonishing and pleasing the simile, and the more likely it is to awaken delight.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p108/r4] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The cited poem makes the blue violet resemble early flames on sulfur tips among red gems; this distant likeness is stranger and more captivating than comparing narcissus to jeweled bowls.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p108/r5] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | An object appearing in an unfamiliar place or form fascinates more; comparing violet to another plant or colored object would lose this strangeness and beauty.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p286#2/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | rejects | Reading the poem as a simple comparison with the known moon absurdly makes that moon light the earth while leaving the speaker's saddle dark.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p286#2/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Al-Buḥturī treats the praised man as an already established moon and invents a new moon-like being with the astonishing trait of leaving one spot dark.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p286#2/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | This rhetorical construction resists كاف, كأن, تحسب, and تخال because those forms introduce an uncertain relation to an otherwise understood predicate.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p286#2/r4] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | These verbs suit a predicate already known in general but uncertainly attached to the subject, or a familiar metaphor; here the described phenomenon itself is unknown.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p320/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Calling the earth alive refers figuratively to its greenness, freshness, and flowering, while saying that God revives it is a literal attribution.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p64/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Wealth is sought for beneficial use, not possession alone; a rich miser who never benefits from it is poor in the relevant sense.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p64/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · اللؤماء | rejects | The claim that a miser still benefits from imagined future access or a sense of security is rejected as wishful self-excuse; wealth can instead bring humiliation and torment.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p64/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The author compares this excuse to an oppressor boasting of power: the one who validates such a boast is more blameworthy than the one who denies it and hopes for the oppressor's reform.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p64/r4] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Contentment is genuine wealth and greed makes its possessor poor; this is substantively true even when phrased as a comparison.

0/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | A coordinated set of clauses functioning as a condition must be parsed jointly; its parts form one grammatical whole, just as both parts of a predicate, adjective, or circumstantial phrase do.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p242/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari reports that al-Kindi called three forms redundant; Abu al-Abbas answered that they respectively assert, answer a question, and answer a denial, so their meanings differ.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p242/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The particle إن binds the following clause to what precedes so the two cohere as one utterance; removing it makes them separate, and فاء does not restore the same relation.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p242/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · بشار | reports | Bashshar’s line about starting early uses إن to show how the second clause becomes closely integrated with the first.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p242/r4] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · بعض العرب | reports | An anonymous Arab’s line about camel-song supplies a second poetic example of إن joining the clauses into a cohesive statement.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p275/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Rhetorical merit belongs to the form in which meaning is expressed, not to bare words as sounds; descriptions such as elegance or ornament name qualities of that form and its effect on meaning.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p387/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Adding an object changes a transitive verb’s meaning rather than appending a separate fact; the object shapes what action is asserted, as an adjective shapes a noun’s reference.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p387/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The proverb about a person’s speech and courage, and the example إن أتاك زيد أتاك لحاجة, illustrate how the second verb can acquire a distinct sense through its added qualification or object.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p91/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The image of the neighborhood's ravines flowing toward him gains its beauty from the original placement of the adverbials; rearranging them removes its sweetness and emotional effect.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p91/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | A passage may gain merit from wording, from composition, or from both; when both contribute, readers often wrongly credit the wording alone, and metaphorical merit may require understanding نظم.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p91/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The force of واشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا is not metaphor alone: the verb is predicated of something related to the true agent, شيبا, which follows in the accusative to clarify that relation. | mentions 19:4
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p175#2/r5] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The earth is khāshiʿa when it is dry, dusty, and without vegetation.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p175#2/r6] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Water makes the earth stir and swell; the One who revives it is able to raise the dead and is powerful over everything.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p17/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الجمهور | reports | The majority read rabbat.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p17/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو جعفر بن القعقاع والرؤاسي عن أبي عمرو | reports | Abu Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ reads rabāʾat with hamza; al-Ruʾasi reports the same from Abu ʿAmr. It means rose or became elevated, like al-rabīʾa, a lookout set on high ground.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p17/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The revival of dead earth is the sign by which people should infer that God can revive the dead.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p17/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The statement is general, and in the language a “thing” means an existent.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p17/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The parched earth’s drooping and roughness under drought and scorching wind make it look downcast, like someone nearly weeping; its revival points from a visible sign to resurrection.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p17/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The earth’s khushūʿ is its visible barrenness and roughness during drought and the dryness of scorching winds.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p17/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The water sent down is rain.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p17/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The earth’s movement is its parts loosening with water and cracking open for plants.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p17/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Rabwahā means its swelling with water and the rise of its surface.
[TABRISI:41:36-39/r20] TABRISI, d. 548 · قتادة والسدي | reports | Qatāda and al-Suddī explain the humbled earth as dusty, worn out, and broken down.
[TABRISI:41:36-39/r21] TABRISI, d. 548 · قيل | reports | Another explanation calls it dead and dry with no vegetation; al-Azharī says dry earth without rain is described as humbled.
[TABRISI:41:36-39/r22] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | When water falls, the earth stirs with vegetation, swells, and rises before the plants sprout.
[TABRISI:41:39-42/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbi explains that the earth stirs with vegetation and grows through abundant crop yield.
[TABRISI:41:39-42/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God revived the earth with rain and will likewise revive the dead at the resurrection.
[TABRISI:41:39-42/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God is capable of everything.
[RAZI-FULL:v27p112#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “Humble” means subdued and diminished; the word is metaphorically applied to earth when it lacks rain and vegetation.
[RAZI-FULL:v27p112#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The earth stirs with new growth and swells as plants approach emergence, lifting and splitting the soil.
[RAZI-FULL:v27p112#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The One who revives dead earth can revive dead bodies; the earth’s renewal is evidence for bodily resurrection.
[RAZI-FULL:v27p112#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Reassembling scattered bodily parts is possible, as is restoring life, intellect, and ability to them; since God can do all possibilities, bodily resurrection is plainly possible.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:37-39/r19] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The address is to every rational person; dry, barren earth is a sign that God brings the dead back to life.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:39/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | A khāshiʿa land is gray and grows vegetation; a khāshiʿ town or place is dusty and uninhabited.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:39/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | A further view treats swelling and shaking as one state: the emergence of vegetation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:39/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-Qurṭubī links this revival-of-earth argument to the treatment of the same meaning in Sūrat al-Ḥajj. | mentions 22:5
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:39/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The God who revives dead earth will revive the dead, for He has power over everything.

[QURTUBI-FULL:41:39/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الشاعر | reports | A poet compares a person shaking for generosity to a sword blade quivering for dew, illustrating the sense of movement in ihtazz.

[QURTUBI-FULL:41:39/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Shaking and swelling may occur before shoots emerge or after plants reach the surface; growth raises the earth, while vegetation first moves outward and then expands in height, length and width.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:39/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Rabat can mean rising, as shown by the names rabwa and rābiya for raised ground.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:39/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو جعفر وخالد | reports | Abū Jaʿfar and Khālid read warabaʾat with hamza, meaning that the earth grew or increased, from al-rabīʾa.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:39/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Another explanation says the earth rejoices at rain when it shakes and swells with vegetation; since splitting for plants is described as laughing, the earth may likewise be described as rejoicing.

[BAYDAWI-FULL:41:38-40/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | After rain, the earth is adorned with growth and swells.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:41:38-40/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | A variant reads ربأت, meaning rose or increased.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:41:38-40/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The One reviving the dead earth will revive the dead and can do everything, including give life and death.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p91#4/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The earth is dry and changed; khushūʿ literally denotes submission and is applied metaphorically to barren land with no growth.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p91#4/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The water is rain; the earth stirs with vegetation and swells.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p91#4/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The One who revived the earth will necessarily be able to resurrect the dead, since He has power over everything.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p182#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | A barren, plantless earth revives and produces varied crops and fruits after rain; its revival demonstrates God’s power to resurrect the dead and His power over all things.
[NASHR:v2p325/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو جعفر | reports | Abu Ja'far reads rabat with an added open hamza after bāʾ in both this verse and Fussilat; the other

[BIQAI-FULL:v6p577/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | After signs in heaven, some of which are worshiped, the passage turns to earthly signs; unlike Yasin, the context here emphasizes oneness, while Yasin stresses resurrection and the earth’s proof is clearer there. | mentions 36:33
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p577/r10] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The visible revival of earth proves power to bring the nonexistent into being and restore what decayed and crumbled; reviving the dead is no different.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p577/r11] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | God revives the dead just as He brings forth plants after they decayed and became soil.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p577/r12] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Although people acknowledge God’s complete power, their denial of resurrection treats Him as unable; all possible things are equally within complete power.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p577/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | One sees part of the earth directly and apprehends the rest by reasoning from what is visible, since all of it is equally within divine power.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p577/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The earth is “humble” when dry and bare of vegetation, like a powerless, flattened person.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p577/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Biqāʿī says this depiction is closer to the worshipper’s state than the description previously used in al-Hajj. | mentions 22:5
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p577/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | God’s sending of rain is exclusively His act and one of the strongest signs of the One; the switch to the majestic plural signals power and greatness.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p577/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Rain may come from clouds or be driven from high places, bringing soil suitable for growth even to saline land such as Egypt.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p577/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The earth “shakes” by moving greatly, abundantly, and quickly, as though it were doing this of its own accord.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p577/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The earth cracks and rises; plants emerge, cover its face, branch roots, and thicken stems until passage across it is impeded.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p577/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | As an inward allusion, knowledge waters the soul-earth: remorse bears blessings, shortcomings are pardoned, and obedience, nearness, and divine manifestations adorn and purify it.
[BURSEVI:v8p204#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Ihtazzat means it moved, here by producing vegetation.
[BURSEVI:v8p204#2/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Hearts revive through faith's light, sincere seeking, and strong longing when grace's rain and mercy water them.
[BURSEVI:v8p204#2/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعض الصالحين | reports | A righteous observer says he saw Samnūn swaying during the circumambulation; at a question about standing before God, Samnūn fainted and, on waking, recited a poem.
[BURSEVI:v8p204#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The ground swells as a plant nears emergence, then rises and splits; rabā means to increase and grow, and a horse may swell after running or fright.

[BURSEVI:v8p204#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The earth's life-giving is really the stirring of its growth powers and renewal of its freshness through varied plants.
